vignette:
Ricardo, at 75, carries himself with the quiet dignity of a man who has spent decades ensuring precision and reliability. As a QA engineer, his world was one of meticulous checks, identifying potential failures, and building robust systems. His home, shared with his wife, Sofia, for over fifty years, was an extension of this philosophy – a place of order, comfort, and predictable routines. They enjoyed their retirement years, tending to their garden, hosting family, and taking evening strolls along the coast. Life, he believed, was largely within one's ability to manage and secure.

Then came the hurricane. It was a monster, unlike anything he had witnessed in his lifetime. The initial warnings brought his usual methodical preparation: securing loose items, stocking supplies, reviewing their evacuation plan. But the storm’s fury far exceeded any contingency. He remembers the wind, a primal shriek that seemed to tear at the very fabric of reality, not just their house. He remembers the terrifying sound of the roof groaning, then peeling away in sections, like paper. He remembers holding Sofia’s hand in the hallway, the only place left that felt somewhat secure, as water began to seep under the doors, reflecting the flashes of lightning outside. He felt utterly helpless, a feeling alien to him, as the carefully constructed edifice of his life, both physical and metaphorical, crumbled around them. The night was an eternity of terror, the constant question gnawing at him: Will we survive this? Can I protect her?

They did survive, evacuated by boat the next morning, witnessing a landscape transformed into unrecognizable devastation. Their beloved home was severely damaged, but they were alive. Yet, for Ricardo, the storm never truly left.

Now, months later, the world feels fundamentally altered. The meticulous engineer who once found comfort in order finds himself trapped in a new kind of disorder. The slightest change in weather – a strong gust of wind, a sudden downpour – sends a jolt of ice through his veins. He catches himself bracing, his muscles tensing, as if the house is about to give way again. He sees flashes of the hurricane, not just in his mind's eye but almost overlaid on the present moment: the swirling dark water, the splintered wood, the frantic, panicked look on Sofia’s face. These intrusive images often hijack his thoughts, especially when he’s trying to focus on something else, like a crossword puzzle or a conversation with his grandchildren.

Sleep offers little respite. Nightmares are frequent and vivid. He wakes in a cold sweat, the roar of the wind still echoing in his ears, feeling the desperate urge to check on Sofia, even though she is sleeping soundly beside him. He often lies awake for hours afterwards, replaying snippets of that night, unable to shake the feeling of impending doom.

He finds himself avoiding anything that might trigger these memories. He quickly changes the channel if a news report mentions hurricanes or natural disasters. He no longer enjoys their walks along the coast, finding the vastness of the ocean unsettling, a reminder of uncontrolled power. He’s stopped working on his small home projects, the very tasks that once brought him satisfaction, because the tools and materials remind him of the repairs needed on their damaged house, a constant, tangible reminder of the trauma. He also finds himself increasingly distant from Sofia. While she was there with him, he feels a chasm between them now, a sense that no one can truly understand the fear he experienced, or the profound sense of failure he carries for not being able to "engineer" their safety.

His meticulous nature, once a strength, has morphed into a debilitating hypervigilance. He obsessively checks weather forecasts, scrutinizing every isobar and wind speed prediction. He now has three emergency kits, each more detailed than the last, strategically placed throughout the house. Every creak of the old house, every unfamiliar sound, sends him on an investigative mission, convinced it’s a sign of impending structural failure or another disaster. He startles easily, jumping at the sudden ring of the phone or a car backfiring outside.

At work, where he still consults part-time, his concentration is shot. He struggles to review complex schematics, his mind drifting back to the chaos. He finds himself irritable, snapping at younger colleagues when they don’t adhere to his increasingly rigid standards, convinced that any deviation is a precursor to catastrophic failure. He feels a pervasive sense of dread, a belief that the world is inherently unsafe, and that no amount of planning or quality assurance can truly protect anyone. The joy he once found in his life, in his work, in his family, feels muted, overshadowed by a persistent, gnawing anxiety that another storm is always just over the horizon.
